video_title: Should we feel good about the trajectory of clean energy post-Trump?
gist: Lily Burmel, author of the MIT CEEPR 'Glass half full' commentary, walks host David Roberts through Energy Innovation modeling showing that after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act repealed most IRA power-sector support, roughly 74% of the clean capacity, 71% of clean generation and 67% of the emissions reductions that the IRA-plus-regulations trajectory would have delivered still show up over the coming decade — with distributed solar (95% preserved) and batteries resilient and onshore wind the casualty at 47%. She argues the surviving momentum means Democrats should prioritize zero-cost permitting reform and clean-firm commercialization over re-extending wind and solar tax credits, while Roberts pushes back that the losses (2.8 gigatons of cumulative CO2, 44 lost deployment-years by 2035) are large and that conceding tax credits lets Republicans define the space of the possible.

insights.claim: Energy Innovation modeling compiled in Lily Burmel's MIT CEEPR commentary finds that 74% of the clean capacity and 71% of the clean generation the IRA-plus-power-plant-regulations trajectory would have delivered still shows up on the US grid over the coming decade under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: The base case for US clean-energy deployment volumes through 2035 is far closer to the IRA case than headline repeal narratives imply, arguing against pricing developer and supply-chain equities off a collapse scenario.
insights.quote: 74% uh will still show up on the grid

insights.claim: 67% of the power-sector emissions reductions expected under the IRA plus Biden power plant regulations still occur on average over the coming decade under OB3, per the same modeling comparison.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Sets a quantified floor on US power-sector decarbonization that survives federal policy reversal, relevant to carbon-intensity assumptions in utility and industrial models.
insights.quote: 67% of those will still occur on average over the coming decade

insights.claim: Fossil capacity is only about 4% higher under OB3 than under the IRA trajectory, but the mix shifts toward coal and away from gas, making the fleet more emissions-intensive per unit and producing roughly 19% more emissions via higher generation rather than new build.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: The bearish emissions surprise is coal capacity-factor retention, not a gas build boom — watch coal plant retirement deferrals and coal burn rather than turbine orders.
insights.quote: the capacity in the uh OB3 scenario is 4% higher than the prior trajectory, but the composition changes

insights.claim: Because fossil plants are dispatchable, flat fossil capacity still translates into materially higher emissions as existing units run more hours to fill in for clean energy that never got built.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Existing coal and gas asset owners capture higher run-hours and revenue without capex — a value driver for merchant thermal fleets.
insights.quote: it will run for more hours of the day to fill in for the less clean energy that's built

insights.claim: The cumulative ten-year emissions difference between the IRA and OB3 power-sector scenarios is 2.8 gigatons of CO2, which Burmel calculates is roughly equal to two 2024-sized years of US power sector emissions.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Quantifies the irreversible cost of the policy reversal: unlike deferred deployment, cumulative atmospheric CO2 cannot be recovered later.
insights.quote: that's equal to about two like 2024 sized worth of power sector emissions

insights.claim: Burmel's 'lag analysis' finds solar reaches the IRA-case deployment milestone (about 333 GW in 2031) only about 2.5 years later under OB3, but the report also shows a cumulative 44 lost deployment years on clean capacity and 56 on generation by 2035, with wind averaging 11.5 lost deployment years.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: The same dataset supports both a bullish 'small delay' read and a bearish 'compounding losses' read — investors should specify which horizon they are underwriting.
insights.quote: a cumulative 44 deployment years

insights.claim: Roberts argues the honest framing of the results is that the US gets about 30% less clean energy and roughly a third fewer emissions reductions than under the IRA, which are big absolute hits even if smaller than many feared.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: A reminder that 'better than feared' framing is relative to a collapsed expectation, not to an adequate decarbonization path.

insights.claim: Burmel argues Trump-two clean energy policy is on paper better than Trump-one because it retains clean firm tax credits, more loan programs office funding and a decade of zero-carbon investment that Republicans passed on a party-line trifecta vote.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Federal support for nuclear, geothermal and other clean firm remains durable through a Republican trifecta — a policy-risk asymmetry favoring clean firm over wind and solar.
insights.quote: the Republicans on a trifecta you know partyline vote just agreed to create investments and spend money on zerocarbon technology for a decade

themes.theme: Technology Winners and Losers Under OB3

insights.claim: Solar and batteries retain roughly 80% of their IRA-case capacity and generation under OB3, while onshore wind retains only 47% of its capacity — the aggregate 74% figure masks a sharp technology split.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Argues for pair trading solar and storage exposure against onshore wind developers and turbine suppliers rather than treating 'renewables' as one basket.
insights.quote: we only see 47% of its capacity preserved

insights.claim: Distributed solar is the single most resilient clean technology in the model at about 95% of capacity preserved, which Burmel attributes to net metering and other state-level policies plus rising utility-scale prices pushing deployment toward the distributed side.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Residential and commercial solar demand is insulated from federal repeal and driven by state policy — a differentiated exposure versus utility-scale developers.
insights.quote: about 95% of its capacity is preserved

insights.claim: Offshore wind shows 100% preservation in the model only because its pipeline is so small that the model builds all of it, not because the sector is healthy.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: The offshore wind resilience number is a modeling artifact and should not be read as a bullish signal, especially given active federal efforts against those projects.

insights.claim: Onshore wind was already declining before the tax credit repeal because it is severely transmission-constrained, regionally limited, capex-heavy and has not seen the innovation-driven cost declines of solar and batteries.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Wind's weakness is structural, not just fiscal, so restoring credits would not by itself restore the sector's growth trajectory.
insights.quote: wind was already struggling. It was already down and yanking the tax credit was kind of beating it on its way down.

insights.claim: Burmel frames the preservation percentages as a two-part diagnostic: the lost share measures how dependent each technology was on tax credits, and the retained share measures underlying market momentum.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: A reusable test for subsidy dependence that can be applied to any technology facing a credit phase-out.
insights.quote: the difference shows the impact of the credits and then what remains shows the market momentum behind it.

insights.claim: Batteries retained their tax credit under OB3 while also benefiting from continued cost declines, which is a major reason storage held up far better than wind.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Storage has both subsidy support and cost-curve support intact — the cleanest structural growth exposure in the modeled outcome.

insights.claim: Burmel warns that a model is a snapshot of assumptions, not a live forecast, and that anything absent from Energy Innovation's input data — behind-the-meter build, clean firm deals, executive-branch obstruction — is also absent from its outputs.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: A discipline for reading any policy model: check what the inputs track before treating the output as a forecast.
insights.quote: a model is just a camera. It just captures a moment in time of what we think might happen. It's not a thermometer and it's not a live weather forecast.

insights.claim: The Trump administration's whole-of-government campaign against wind and solar permits — including a July 2025 Interior memo requiring the secretary to personally sign off on public-land projects against a 69-item checklist — is a real negative that could not be modeled and was later vacated by a judge.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Regulatory harassment risk is an unmodeled discount to the 74% figure, and legal reversals restore optionality only with a lag.
insights.quote: a 69 line item list

insights.claim: Federal-land obstruction has limited reach because 99% of US wind and 80-90% of US solar is built on private land, though wind remains exposed because every project needs FAA approval.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Bounds the downside from federal permitting attacks for solar while identifying FAA sign-off as wind's specific chokepoint.
insights.quote: 99% of wind is built on private land and 80 to 90% of solar is built on private land as well

insights.claim: Near-term deployment through 2030 is protected by tax-credit safe harboring, a conclusion Burmel says is independently validated by Rhodium Group and Jesse Jenkins' REPEAT lab.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Order books and installation volumes through 2030 are largely locked in; the policy damage shows up in the post-2030 pipeline.
insights.quote: deployment through 2030 is very strong and robust because of that safe harboring

insights.claim: Crux Climate CEO Alfred Johnson's 'light years' framing — what gets deployed today reflects permitting and construction decisions made years ago — implies Trump-era obstruction is bullish for near-term volumes and bearish for the late 2020s and 2030s.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Creates a timing trade: strong reported installations now are a lagging indicator and should not be read as evidence policy damage was overstated.
insights.quote: he calls the grid something like light years

insights.claim: Michael Thomas's Cleanview project database shows that of roughly 90 GW of announced behind-the-meter gas, only about two-thirds have turbine commitments from manufacturers and only about 2 GW has actually been built.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: The headline behind-the-meter gas pipeline is heavily overstated; turbine order commitments, not announcements, are the signal to track.
insights.quote: only twothirds of that might actually have turbines and then only two gigawatts have actually been built so far

insights.claim: Roberts believes behind-the-meter gas projections contain a large element of fantasy because hyperscalers will find that building and operating their own grid is far harder than their models suggest.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: If correct, gas turbine backlogs tied to data-center self-generation carry high cancellation risk.
insights.quote: I think those projections are there's a large element of fantasy to that

insights.claim: Three nuclear restarts — Palisades, Crane and Duane Arnold — will add gigawatts of clean firm capacity within a couple of years, and are not captured in the model's outputs because they are not in Energy Innovation's inputs.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Unmodeled upside to clean generation and downside to coal run-hours in the near term.
insights.quote: the Palisades project crane Duan Arnold

insights.claim: Nuclear license extensions from 60-year to 80-year operating contracts represent a second unmodeled source of preserved clean capacity.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Existing nuclear owners gain decades of additional asset life, supporting valuations independent of new-build economics.
insights.quote: I think a lot of these projects are running for 60 years and we're seeing them revise their contracts to run for 80 years

insights.claim: Google's framework agreement with Fervo Energy to deliver 3 GW of geothermal capacity through 2033 is cited as evidence that hyperscaler willingness to pay for speed is changing clean firm project economics beyond what cost-optimization models assume.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Corporate offtake, not federal subsidy, is becoming the marginal buyer setting clean firm deployment — watch hyperscaler PPAs as the leading indicator.
insights.quote: 3 gawatts of capacity through 2033

insights.claim: Cost-optimization models systematically misprice the current market because hyperscalers value speed to power over least cost, a preference that shows up as behind-the-meter gas and premium-priced clean firm contracts.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Suppliers who can deliver interconnection speed can charge above the modeled cost curve — a margin opportunity outside merit-order logic.
insights.quote: speed to power has a price that companies are willing to pay

themes.theme: Demand Growth as Clean Energy Tailwind

insights.claim: The US is experiencing the fastest energy demand growth since World War II, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's 2026 Queued Up report finds 90% of what was added to the grid last year was clean.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Clean technologies are the default marginal supply regardless of federal subsidy, so demand growth mechanically pulls through clean additions.
insights.quote: 90% of what gets added to the grid last year was clean

insights.claim: The demand wave from electrification — EVs, heat pumps, buildings — will end up as large as or larger than the current data-center-driven demand pull, which Burmel and Roberts argue is being crowded out of the conversation by AI hype.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Grid capex needs persist well beyond any AI capex cycle, supporting a longer-duration thesis on transmission, distribution and generation equipment.
insights.quote: the demand from electrification, clean electrification

insights.claim: Burmel frames today's data-center demand as unusually favorable because it comes from deep-pocketed customers willing to fund grid investment ahead of the later electrification wave.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler capital is effectively subsidizing grid buildout that later electrification demand will use — an argument against 'policing' load growth.
insights.quote: thank God that right now the demand growth that we are seeing is from customers with massive pockets who want to pay and are willing to invest in our grid

insights.claim: Jesse Jenkins found shortly after IRA passage that 80% of the law's 2030 emissions reductions would be lost if transmission could not be built faster, and Burmel notes the US has been building transmission slower ever since that report.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Transmission, not subsidy, is the binding constraint on realized emissions outcomes — the highest-leverage variable to monitor.
insights.quote: 80% of the 2030 emissions reductions from the IRA would be totally lost if we could not build transmission any faster

insights.claim: John Bistline's Nature paper comparing every IRA model found that later assessments produced progressively dimmer outlooks as modelers came to appreciate transmission constraints and the deployment ceiling.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: A systematic bias correction: early policy-impact estimates in this sector trend downward as physical constraints are incorporated.
insights.quote: later assessments of the impact of the IRA had dimmer and dimmer outlooks

insights.claim: The Energy Innovation model contains a hard cap on how much energy can be added in any period reflecting permitting, siting, interconnection and construction gauntlets, so lifting that ceiling would raise both the IRA and OB3 results.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Permitting and interconnection reform is upside optionality that sits outside the 74% figure entirely.

insights.claim: Burmel argues better grid utilization is worth pursuing urgently but is marginal in scale: roughly 40 GW of demand flexibility capacity exists today and Brattle's cited 200 GW of unused grid capacity is only about 15% of the 1,300 GW that doubling the grid would require.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Grid-enhancing technologies and flexibility are real but cannot substitute for physical buildout — sizing matters when valuing GETs and demand-response businesses.
insights.quote: a doubling of the grid would be 1300 gawatt

insights.claim: Roberts counters that grid utilization deserves maximum effort precisely because it could do in the short term what proposed gas buildout is meant to do, while the longer-term wind and solar constraints are being slowly lifted.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: Positions utilization tech as the direct competitor to speed-to-power gas, a substitution to watch as data-center interconnection queues bind.

themes.theme: Permitting Reform vs Tax Credit Extension

insights.claim: Burmel argues permitting reform is the higher-priority federal lever than restoring wind and solar tax credits because it requires zero fiscal space, lowers project costs by reducing delays and cancellations, and can only be achieved through bipartisan compromise that makes it durable.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: If Democrats adopt this prioritization, the next policy cycle favors developers exposed to permitting throughput over those levered to subsidy restoration.
insights.quote: permanent reform I've loved thinking about it recently is like free money

insights.claim: Burmel says comprehensive permitting reform must pass in this Congress because negotiators are close to a final deal and the committee chairs with jurisdiction in the next Congress look less favorable to a bipartisan compromise.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Names a concrete near-term legislative catalyst window with a specific closing mechanism.
insights.quote: negotiators are quite close to be coming to a final deal

insights.claim: Burmel warns that failing to pass permitting reform now means the next administration arrives with an empty toolkit.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Frames the cost of legislative failure as multi-cycle, not merely a one-Congress delay.
insights.quote: the next administration will show up with an embarrassingly empty pantry of tools to use

insights.claim: Burmel argues wind and solar tax credits, despite nearly 50 years of bipartisan extensions, became the sacrificial lamb because they hand Republicans an incoherence attack — that Democrats call clean energy cheapest while still subsidizing it.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Explains why the credits are structurally the most repeal-prone piece of clean energy policy in future cycles.
insights.quote: They've existed for almost 50 years since its inception and always extended on a bipartisan basis

insights.claim: Some Republicans oppose transmission specifically because building it would unlock more subsidized renewables, which Burmel presents as evidence that removing the credits can reduce right-wing opposition to grid buildout.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Implies a policy trade — surrendering wind and solar credits in exchange for transmission — with asymmetric benefit to grid infrastructure builders.
insights.quote: Republicans who will acknowledge that they are against transmission because of the slush fund

insights.claim: Burmel cites center-right grid policy figure Travis Fisher testifying before Congress that the wind and solar tax credit phase-down brought him around to supporting transmission, calling it tangible counter-polarization.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: A concrete data point that a bipartisan transmission coalition is forming post-repeal — the key precondition for permitting legislation.
insights.quote: he testified in front of Congress this year that the phase down of the wind and solar tax credits has made him come around to transmission

insights.claim: Roberts argues that treating Republican reversibility as a reason not to pursue policy is 'DC brain' that lets opponents define the space of the possible, drawing an analogy to abortion and voting rights.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: Flags the durability argument as contested inside the climate policy community, meaning tax credit restoration is not off the table politically.
insights.quote: you are undercover of being savvy and realistic just more or less explicitly allowing your political opponents to define the space of what's permissible and what's allowable

insights.claim: Roberts warns that technocratic center-right think tankers like Travis Fisher are not representative of the governing Republican coalition, which uses a sledgehammer rather than the tweaks those analysts propose.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: Cautions against underwriting bipartisan transmission deals on the strength of think-tank sentiment rather than elected-official behavior.

insights.claim: Burmel contends Republicans actually took a scalpel rather than a sledgehammer to the IRA, preserving every tax credit's duration and amount except wind and solar, applying FEOC restrictions, cutting grants, and keeping the renamed loan office.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: The surviving federal capital stack for nuclear, geothermal, hydrogen and storage is larger than the repeal narrative suggests.
insights.quote: there was no sledgehammer taken to it. It was a scalpel, right? Every single tax credit was preserved in duration and in amount except for wind and solar.

insights.claim: Roberts characterizes the wind and solar carve-out as culture-war symbolism rather than policy conviction, with Republicans taking just enough to own the libs while leaving the rest of the clean energy architecture intact.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: If the driver is symbolic, other clean technologies face lower repeal risk while wind and solar face persistent political targeting.
insights.quote: They just took enough of the chunk out of it to own the libs

themes.theme: Storage vs Clean Firm: The Firmness Argument

insights.claim: Roberts challenges the emerging DC consensus that renewables plus storage can never be firm, arguing that with 8-hour batteries, sodium-ion, new silicon anodes boosting energy density fivefold and long-duration storage, sufficient storage should eventually deliver whatever firmness gas provides.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: If correct, clean firm investment theses that assume an unbridgeable firmness gap are overvaluing nuclear and geothermal relative to storage.
insights.quote: if you get enough storage, why isn't it firm? Like what is the firmness of natural gas that sufficient storage can't get renewable energy to?

insights.claim: Burmel counters that today's 4-hour batteries are insufficient for around-the-clock reliability and that storage shifts the time of generation rather than making power dispatchable on demand, since batteries must be charged first.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Defines the technical distinction underpinning clean firm investment: time-shifting versus true dispatchability.

insights.claim: Burmel identifies land constraints alongside transmission as a reason solar-plus-storage cannot simply scale to power everything, questioning whether Manhattan-sized solar farms for data centers are feasible.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Land and siting, not just battery chemistry, cap the solar-plus-storage substitution for firm capacity.

insights.claim: Burmel's report introduces a shallow-versus-deep decarbonization framing distinguishing technologies that merely reduce fossil generation from those that can supplant fossil capacity outright.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: A useful lens for classifying assets: peak-shaving renewables versus capacity-displacing clean firm carry different terminal values.
insights.quote: shallow versus deep decarbonization

insights.claim: Both agree the US already has enough gas capacity for a high-renewables endgame, and Burmel confirms the models do not build more gas because existing plants can simply ramp up and down.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Directly undercuts the case for a large new gas buildout — new gas capacity additions may be stranded-asset candidates.
insights.quote: we do have enough gas, which is why the models don't build more gas

insights.claim: Variable renewable penetration averages around 40% across grids today and can spike to 70-90% but not on a sustained basis, which Burmel uses to argue for simultaneously raising sustained penetration and commercializing the last-percent technologies.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Quantifies today's real renewable penetration ceiling, a benchmark for judging claims about high-renewables grids.
insights.quote: the average it sits around 40% across all these grids and it can surge and spike up to 70 to 90% but that's not a sustained level

themes.theme: Durable Policy Design and the International Signal

insights.claim: Burmel argues the strongest climate policy is the one that lasts, prioritizing durable consistent decarbonization results over an ambitious law whose impact is hamstrung when it survives only a couple of years.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: A design principle that predicts future Democratic policy will favor bipartisan-durable structures over maximalist spending — changing the shape of the next subsidy cycle.
insights.quote: the strongest climate policy is the one that can last and deliver durable consistent decarb results

insights.claim: The IRA was built for 2021 conditions — Democratic trifecta, zero interest rates, jobs prioritized over inflation, minimal room for bipartisanship — and every one of those conditions has now inverted to affordability politics, high rates, massive demand growth, geopolitical competition and a Republican trifecta.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: The next Democratic energy bill will likely look structurally different from the IRA, so extrapolating IRA-style demand subsidies into future forecasts is a mistake.
insights.quote: the color of the room that we walked in in 2021, it's decorated really really differently this time around

insights.claim: Burmel frames the clean energy downturn as a normal capital-intensive cyclical bust amplified by politically induced headwinds after the frothy zero-rate 2021 peak, and expects the next boom to be bigger than the last.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: A cyclical rather than structural read on the sector drawdown, implying eventual mean reversion for clean energy capital formation.
insights.quote: the boom is always bigger than the last time

insights.claim: Burmel argues tax credits are the wrong instrument for clean firm because a tax credit works best when a market is mature enough to respond to a price signal, whereas early-stage clean firm needs patient capital and long-term debt from the Office of Energy Dominance Financing.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Points to federal debt financing rather than tax equity as the growth channel for nuclear, geothermal and fusion — relevant to where project capital will come from.
insights.quote: a tax credit works best when the market is mature enough to respond to a price signal

insights.claim: An analysis Burmel cites found solar has received 50 times as much cumulative federal energy technology support as geothermal.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Frames geothermal as structurally under-supported, supporting the case for a large future reallocation of federal dollars toward it.
insights.quote: solar has received 50 times as much as geothermal

insights.claim: Burmel calls the methane fee underrated because its revenue sources extend beyond ten years, which made it legally hard for Republicans to repeal — an example of repeal-resistant policy design.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: A concrete template for structuring climate policy to survive party turnover, worth watching in the design of future bills.
insights.quote: the methane fee I think is pretty underrated that it was able to survive because it has revenue sources beyond 10 years

insights.claim: Assuming the endangerment finding is effectively dead, Burmel names four fossil regulatory measures she believes the oil and gas industry generally supports: reinstating the methane fee, expanding carbon credit support, restoring the greenhouse gas reporting program, and using that data for a carbon tariff and product-level carbon intensity standards.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Maps the plausible next-cycle regulatory surface for fossil producers — carbon intensity disclosure and border adjustment rather than emissions caps.
insights.quote: reinstating the greenhouse gas reporting program

insights.claim: Roberts pushes back on the durability framing as a recurring trap in which Republicans break institutions and spend the money, then Democrats trim their ambitions to fit the wreckage instead of reversing it.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: Signals real intra-coalition disagreement over whether the next Democratic energy bill is modest or maximalist.

insights.claim: Burmel responds that she translates ambition into results and rejects performative austerity, while insisting a colorful, massive climate law that lasts only a couple of years is worth less than smaller durable policy.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Crystallizes the results-over-ambition doctrine likely to shape the next Democratic energy platform.
insights.quote: Like I want results more than I want ambition.

insights.claim: Rhodium Group analysis cited by Burmel found the IRA's emissions reduction benefits would be 2 to 4 times larger in the rest of the world than domestically, because US innovation and commercialization diffuse technology abroad.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Reframes US clean energy policy as an export-driven global lever, supporting a thesis around American clean tech diffusion rather than domestic emissions alone.
insights.quote: the emissions reductions benefits of the IRA would be larger in the rest of the world by 2 to 4x compared to here at home

insights.claim: Burmel argues international trust in the US is damaged for reasons far deeper than climate, so repair should run through innovation diffusion, trade, investment and foreign assistance rather than through the Paris Agreement and UNFCCC process.
insights.speaker: Lily Burmel
insights.so_what: Suggests the next administration's climate leverage will show up in trade and export finance policy, not multilateral pledges.
insights.quote: other countries are upset with America for reasons far worse than climate and far deeper than climate
